## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

<br>By the end of this lecture you should be able to:

- Explain how cellular heterogeneity impacts measurements of drug responses.
- Explain how tissue spatial organization impacts measurements of drug responses.
- Use cell-specific molecular signatures to evaluate and screen pharmacological responses.
- Compare cell-specific dose-response relationships to tissue-level measurements for evaluating drug efficacy and safety.

<!-- ======================================================================
     INTRO — RECAP + HUB
     ====================================================================== -->

## LOSING HETEROGENEITY IN THE AVERAGES

<br>In the last lecture we examined signatures measured from a **whole piece of tissue** or measured in <i>bulk</i>. That number is an average over every cell and every location in the sample.

- Different cell types respond to the same drug in different ways.
- Cells sit in organized neighborhoods, and location changes their exposure and behavior.
- An average can hide a strong response in a small group of cells.

## TISSUES ARE MIXTURES OF CELL TYPES {#l2-heterogeneity}

<br>A bulk RNA-seq measurement is a **weighted average** of every cell in the sample, weighted by how many cells of each type there are and how much RNA each makes. For example:

- A liver sample contains hepatocytes, but also immune, endothelial, and stellate cells.
- A change in the average does not tell you which cell type changed.

::: back-to-hub
<a href="#/l2-hub">↩ Back to menu</a>
:::

## SAME BULK CHANGE, DIFFERENT STORIES

<br>Two very different things can produce the same change in a bulk signature:

- **Composition**: the drug changed *how many* cells of a type are present (for example, immune cells moved into the tissue)
- **State**: the drug changed *what each cell does*, with the same number of cells

## MEASURING CELLS ONE AT A TIME

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="25%"}
Emerging technologies such as single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq measure expression separately in thousands of individual cells. Each column of the heatmap is one cell and each cluster is a cell type with its own marker genes.
::::

:::: {.column .tall-figure width="75%"}
![](../assets/figures/snrna-heatmap.png){fig-alt="Heatmap of single-nucleus RNA-seq data from liver. Columns are individual nuclei grouped into 18 numbered clusters (cell types); rows are marker genes. Each cluster lights up a different block of genes, for example hepatocyte genes in cluster 1 and immune genes in clusters 7 to 9." fig-align="center"}
::::
:::::

::: source-credit
Source: <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2023.1200114" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Li et al. (2023) Front. Pharmacol.</a>
:::

<iframe class="activity-iframe" loading="lazy" title="Bulk or Mixed? Composition versus state activity" src="../activities/composition-vs-state/index.html?seed=2027">

</iframe>

::: notes
A toy liver of 10 cells by 10 genes; bulk is the average of the cells. Step 1 (no lock-in): slide the number of immune cells and watch the bulk row. Immune genes rise and hepatocyte genes dilute. Step 2: keep 2 immune cells in 10 and turn up the immune genes inside each immune cell; only the immune genes move. Step 3: Story A (more immune cells) and Story B (same cells, matching increase in immune gene expression) give the same bulk signal for the immune genes, so bulk alone cannot tell composition from state. The only clue is the small dilution of the hepatocyte genes in Story A, which is lost in real-world variability. This is the first activity, so allow about 10 minutes.
:::

## LOCATION CHANGES THE RESPONSE {#l2-spatial}

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="33%"}
Cells in a tissue are arranged in organized neighborhoods, and cells of the same type can behave differently depending on where they are. For example, in the liver, cells near the central vein and cells near the portal vein express different sets of genes.
::::

:::: {.column .tall-figure width="67%"}

## MEASURING EXPRESSION IN SPACE

<br>Spatial transcriptomics keeps track of where each measurement came from.

- **Spot-based** methods capture a small area that can hold several cells, so a spot is a small mixture
- **Imaging-based** methods read out genes at the level of single cells or molecules, often with a targeted gene panel
- Resolution, number of genes, and cost trade off against each other

::: notes
A 20 by 20 piece of liver, one dot per cell (blue hepatocyte, red immune cell). Raise the percentage of immune cells; in "clustered" mode they form foci, as in inflammation. Three views of the same tissue: the dot map (where the cells are), a compressed single-cell heatmap of 10 genes (rows are genes, each column is a cell, sorted by type with the immune cells first; the red-block of immune genes grows as you add immune cells), and the bulk column, which is all those cells averaged into one column of 10 genes. Ask what the immune genes look like in the heatmap compared with bulk: they are diluted. Then switch between clustered and scattered: the dots change, but the heatmap and the bulk column do not, because expression on its own does not say where the cells are.
:::

## CELL-SPECIFIC SIGNATURES {#l2-signatures}

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="33%"}
Once cells are separated, each cell type can be seen to have its <i>own</i> pattern of gene expression.
::::

:::: {.column .tall-figure width="67%"}
![](../assets/figures/cell-number-deg.png){fig-alt="Upset-style bar chart of the number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in each combination of liver cell types. The tallest bars are genes changed in a single cell type; far fewer genes are shared across all cell types. Circles mark shared, cell-specific, and distinct responses." fig-align="center"}
::::
:::::

## SCREENING WITH CELL-SPECIFIC SIGNATURES

<br>The signature matching from bulk approaches still applies:

- Compare a compound's response in the cell type of interest with known drugs.
- Look for the effect in the intended cell type and for off-target effects in the others.
- A tissue-level match can miss a response that only one cell type shows.

## TISSUE-LEVEL DOSE-RESPONSE CAN MISLEAD {#l2-dose-response}

<br>If only a fraction of the cells respond, the tissue-level curve shows only a fraction of that response.

- A strong response in a small group of cells looks weak in the average.
- The apparent threshold shifts to higher doses, or the response drops below detection altogether.
- A rare, sensitive cell type can be the real target of toxicity.

::: back-to-hub
<a href="#/l2-hub">↩ Back to menu</a>
:::

## CELL- AND SPATIAL-LEVEL DOSE-RESPONSE MODELING

<br>This is an actively evolving field, and much of what we have discussed is still largely theoretical. Single-cell and spatial data pose unique challenges for dose-response modeling.

- The data are very sparse, with many zeroes, which creates statistical challenges.
- There is limited data to develop and test these methods. Single-cell methods are now more affordable (~10X the cost of bulk approaches), but spatial methods are not yet highly scalable (~100–1000X the cost of bulk approaches).

## ACTIVITY: Cell vs. Tissue Dose-Response (LO 4)

::: activity-embed-controls
<button onclick="EmbedBridge.reloadIframe(this)">

::: activity-embed
<iframe class="activity-iframe" loading="lazy" title="Cell-specific versus tissue-level dose-response activity" src="../activities/cell-specific-dose-response/index.html?seed=2030">

</iframe>
:::

::: notes
Start with the bulk dose-response curve for Gene X and the dashed line at 10% response: one curve, one dose. Tick "Split into cell types" to reveal the four curves it is built from: one cell type is far more sensitive than the bulk value suggests (a small population hidden by the average), and one barely responds in this dose range. Untick it and tick "Split into regions" instead: the liver has a portal and a central region, and central hepatocytes are much more sensitive, so the tissue splits into two curves with two different 10% doses. Tick both to see a portal and a central curve for every cell type (eight curves, central ones dashed). The dose slider shows each curve's response at a chosen dose; at the bulk 10% dose, the most sensitive curve is already well above 10%. A new seed changes which cell types are sensitive.
:::

## PUTTING IT TOGETHER

<br>Four objectives, four activities:

- **LO 1** — A tissue measurement averages over cell types, so composition and state changes can look alike.
- **LO 2** — Location shapes the response, and capture area decides what you can see.
- **LO 3** — Cell-specific signatures let you screen for the effect you want, in the cells you want.
- **LO 4** — Cell-specific dose-response can reveal sensitivity that the tissue average hides.
